RagShortTexts: Carcassonne with its double circuit walls and 52 towers cemented royal Capetian control in.

Variants.Content: After the Albigensian Crusade, the Crown turned Carcassonne into one of the strongest fortresses in the south, taking it from the Trencavel viscounts who had lost their lands to the northern army. Under Louis IX and his successors, engineers laid out an inner and an outer circuit of stone walls, with fifty-two towers, flanking galleries, and deep moats that crossbowmen could sweep from either wall. The lower town was walled separately, and the Pyrenean frontier was covered by a chain of castles behind it. The stone was quarried and hauled from nearby hills, and that labour fell heavily on the cantons around the city. Masons, carpenters, and guards drew wages from royal accounts, but the men who worked the quarries and carts rarely saw either the pay or the defences it bought.

The ramparts of Carcassonne told every southern baron that independence had ended. The king's seneschal held the garrison and the keys, answering to Paris rather than to any local count. Any intrigue with the Crown of Aragon was watched from the towers, and a seneschal's letter could summon troops within days.
Building those double walls emptied the quarry tithes of whole cantons. Common folk must live in the lower town; once the iron portcullis drops at dusk, crossbow sentries patrol through the dawn.
